speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the immediate need for the government to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms by giving consideration to the disallowance to date of Bill No. 1, an amendment to the labour relations act, and Bill No. 2, the trade union (emergency provisions) act, as passed by the Newfoundland legislature.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulion (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I refer Your Honour to citation 161 at page 135 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which I submit clearly disposes of the matter. The citation commences:
Disallowance of provincial laws is not one of the functions of the dominion parliament.
I now refer to the second paragraph of that citation:
Since the only power enjoyed by our House of Commons in matters of disallowance is to criticize the action of the dominion government after it has either disallowed or refused to disallow a provincial act. it follows that the house must await government action before taking the matter up. If the house considered the act before the expiration of the one-year period during which council must give its decision, it would exceed its own jurisdiction.
There are a number of other paragraphs in this citation which I submit clearly establish that a motion of this type is out of order.

subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
On the point of order which has been raised by the Minister of Justice, the minister has pointed out that this citation reads in part as follows:
-it follows that the house must await government action before taking the matter up.
We have awaited that government action. We have awaited that action for the whole period of one year. This is the time when the government should act; and because we have waited for the government to act, and because this is the last day when such a motion as this can be raised, we are presenting it at this time. The citation goes on to say:
If the house considered the act before the expiration of the one-year period during which council must give its decision, it would exceed its own jurisdiction.
It may be a matter of minutes as to when the exact period of one year has elapsed, but today is one year from the day on which the bills were delivered to the cabinet, and we
[Mr. Boivin.l
feel that this is the time when this question should be debated and that this is the proper action to take.
Citation No. 100 on page 89 says that the matter so raised must be within the administrative responsibility of the government. There is no question about that; the government has the responsibility and the jurisdiction to disallow such an act. Paragraph 2 of the same citation reads in part as follows:
The "definite matter of urgent public importance", for the discussion of which the adjournment of the house may be moved under standing order 26, must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention.
I suggest that this matter is very much in this category and that if action is not taken at this time then fundamental rights and human freedoms of Canadian citizens, on this occasion in the province of Newfoundland, will have been abrogated and infringed upon. We therefore feel it is urgent that this matter be considered and that these fundamental rights of Canadian citizens should be protected by the appropriate action of disallowance by the federal government.

subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
May I speak to the point of order which was raised by the Minister of Justice. I suggest, first of all, that the minister broke off too conveniently when he read from page 136. If he had continued to the third paragraph he would have found that the words immediately following the words he quoted read as follows:
When the year within which disallowance may take place has expired, the government's action or inaction may be discussed in the House of Commons.
If my information is correct the bill was sent to the Secretary of State on March 16, 1959-received on March 16, 1959-and I suggest that the year then expired at midnight last night, so it is not a matter of minutes with respect to the period.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The motion itself, as I recall it-I have not seen a copy yet-asked for the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the desirability of the government taking action now, before it is too late, to disallow this bill. The words of the motion were to that effect. Thus the whole basis on which the motion was moved was that this is in fact the last day. Whether or not my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River would be right in his assumption that midnight last night was the expiry time, the fact of the matter is that if the time has expired the motion is self defeating.
I think the better view would be that one year from the time of receipt-since the

legislation was received on the 16th-would include today. I take it that is the basis upon which the motion was drawn, and without going into the question that is the point to which I was addressing myself. I would refer the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River to the next sentence after the one he stopped at, that sentence reading:
The practice usually followed has been to wait until the question of disallowance has been decided upon by the government and then to move for the production of papers relating thereto.
That is the usual way in which this kind of matter is dealt with.

subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the words of the Minister of Justice. This is an important matter of procedure and the authority of the government. If it is not possible to raise this question until after the time has expired, then of course the government has no authority whatever. All we are asking is that it be recognized that it does have the authority now.

subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I could just say a word, it seems to me it is difficult to conceive that there could be a 16th of March twice in one year. I submit that the argument of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is irrefutable, and that once more the C.C.F. has missed the bus.

speechtext:
The motion which I am asked to accept under rule 26 is to call upon the governor in council, in whom is entrusted under the British North America Act the power of disallowing provincial statutes, to disallow two bills of the legislature of Newfoundland the period of disallowance for which appears to expire today or tomorrow, according to various interpretations of the time. In my view it does not matter whether it expires today or tomorrow. If this is a question of disallowance it is a power which has been entrusted to the executive and not to the legislature. For that reason it seems to be clearly settled and decided in our practice, as stated by Beauchesne in citation No. 161, that until the government has acted the legislature is not competent to call on the government to take one course of action or the other.
Motions for Papers
It is, of course, open to the legislature of Newfoundland to change its laws if it sees fit, and of course it is open to this house to criticize the government if it does not disallow. Such a motion could be brought in the house, in accordance with the citation to which I am referred, criticizing the government tomorrow or on the next supply motion or at any time any hon. member can claim the time of the house for presenting such a motion, so what is in a question here is not criticism of the government for the action it has taken; it is rather a question of seeking to advise the government before it has acted. I think the authority is sufficiently clear that if today is the last day it is too early to bring the motion, and if the time for disallowance has expired the matter has no urgency because any action of the house would not alter the situation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is the very point. Do I understand from what you have just said that the House of Commons cannot deal with this matter until the last minute of the period of authority of the cabinet to deal with the matter; and, if so, that we cannot even raise it then because by that time the time has expired and it is a fait accompli? Is that the case?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is precisely the situation. Perhaps I did not make myself as clear as I should. It is based on the legal responsibility of the government for this action and the corresponding lack of responsibility on the part of the house, so the decision whether or not to disallow is entirely a matter for the government. The house is free to criticize the government. The house is in no position Itself to take a decision or to insist on a decision being taken by the government.

subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You also agree that until the time is up it cannot be questioned, and then it is too late; so where the heck is responsible government?

subtopic: MOTION FOR AD- JOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I do not think it would be appropriate to enter into a debate with the hon. member, but I would be glad to discuss it with him at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was amazed many times yesterday at the speech made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) but no statement of his surprised me more than when he asked the rhetorical question: why has housing been cut back this year? His answer was: "so that the Minister of Finance can balance the budget." The hon. member will find that at page 2108 of Hansard. I am surprised that a veteran of parliamentary life-and the hon. member for Assiniboia has been in the house for 15 years-should have asked such a question. One might think he would know better by this time and be aware that the money used by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make loans to the Canadian public has nothing whatever to do with the budget. If the hon. gentleman did not know that yesterday, he knows it today, and he can always be learning.
We are not spending this money, we are lending it. The only expenditures that enter into the budget are those made under section 23 of the act, in respect of slum clearance, and under section 36 for redevelopment programs such as subsidized housing. Only these expenditures are considered in the budget. Thus, for the benefit of the hon. member for Assiniboia, the leader of the C.C.F. group, this debate is on the subject of loans, not expenditure-loans of $150 million to $175 million, without restricting in any way the money we spend on slum clearance and redevelopment, and we do not expect there will be any cut-back in these expenditures.
It may be, of course, that the lack of knowledge-I am putting it very mildly-on the part of the hon. member for Assiniboia with regard to this subject is due to his socialist upbringing and to the fact that he comes from the province of Saskatchewan which, due to the actions of its government, has very little experience in connection with farm loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This is by reason of the Saskatchewan farm security act which would make it impossible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, if it made a loan to a farmer in the province, to foreclose in the event of default. That is the situation, and it may be the excuse for lack of information on the subject by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) also asked a rhetorical question. Why are you spending only $170 million out of the $500 million, he asked. In the first place, we are not spending this money, we are lending it. In the second place, we are doing so because the government has decided to reduce its borrowing from the capital market of Canada, and for this reason: every time we go into the capital market for a loan there is that much less money available to the provinces and the municipalities. Hon. members on the other side of the house have complained bitterly at times about the difficulties of the municipalities. By reducing our borrowing we are increasing the opportunity open to those municipalities to get money on the capital market. I would also point out that the lending this year-to between $150 million and $175 million-would be approximately the same as the loans made in 1959, save and except the loans made to builders in connection with the winter program which amounted to 14,000 starts.
Another reason why we are setting up an estimate of expenditure of between $150 million and $175 million is that because we are cautious. After two and a half years of a very heavy building program, with 400,000 new houses added to Canada's housing stock and with 82,000 more houses in the process of being built at the present time, we are anxious about over-extending this program. To all members of the house may I give this message: it is too early to say with any finality what the effect of the high interest rate on housing will be. Incidentally, there are high interest rates all over the world today. We may have to change our policy during the year in the light of conditions which we do not anticipate at this time. But as the picture does unfold, hon. members can be sure that the government will give it the most careful and earnest consideration. We intend at the present time, however, to confine our loans in the area between $150 million and $175 million.
As I said before, there is nothing that gives me, as minister in Charge, greater concern than the operation of this policy, which is under continuous review by the government throughout the year. We will take into consideration the state of the housing market, the conditions of general investment in the mortgage market, and the situation of the approved lenders. May I say one thing more. In spite of the encouragement which certain members of the opposition have given to an increase in the N.H.A. interest rate, there will be no increase in the rate of 6f per cent. Most hon. members will be

glad to learn this. In addition, we have no objection if some of the approved lenders wish to reduce the interest rate.
In answer to the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Pascoe) who, by the way, comes from the socialist province of Saskatchewan, may I say that as soon as the socialist government there gets rid of the restrictions on collecting farm mortgage debts we would be very glad to take applications from his riding, and I am sure the result will be just as happy as that of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) in the province of Alberta who boasted of the success of the direct C.M.H.C. loans in many of the small communities in his area.
To the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) may I say that we shall be happy to entertain an application from Whitehorse in his famous riding in connection with a low rental scheme. These will be given the most earnest consideration.
To the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) who suggested loans on a 50-year term, may I respectfully point out to him that 50 years is a long time in the adult life of a man, and we cannot get any support from any approved lender for this kind of loan.
The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Regnier) very properly and very ably suggested that we should participate in arranging shelters against atomic fallout. May I say that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has already undertaken to design and prepare a pamphlet dealing with fallout shelters suitable for new houses, and the corporation is also participating in the testing of a shelter suitable for existing houses.
These helpful suggestions from hon. members are very much appreciated by me as the minister in charge and, as I stated a month ago, I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland) who I have always found to be a very pleasant gentleman. But a great change overtook him yesterday. I cannot believe that it was the same person, except that he still appeared to be good-natured. Nevertheless, his remarks belied that good nature. Instead of a constructive speech, we heard a purely partisan, critical, carping speech.

Having sat on the opposition benches and having become familiar with the attitude of the old government toward this problem of housing, and having become familiar with this government's policy, I would say that this government is going to greater pains to improve the housing program started by the old government. What bothers me is the same thing that bothered the premier of my province when he brought the problem up at the last federal-provincial conference shortly after this government came to office.
The problem in my area is, has been and will continue to be, unless we take measures to change it, the fact that the majority of our people do not have a down payment with which to purchase a house. I went into this problem very thoroughly the other day, so I will not refer to it at length now. However, I should like to submit, very briefly, this proposition to the government, that a new philosophy on the part of the government in connection with housing is a definite requirement in Canada today.
I feel we should adopt the same philosophy toward housing as the United States has adopted. This would mean that the over-all cost of a home to prospective purchasers would not necessarily be determined by the cost of the house, that is whether the house cost $12,000, $15,000 or $18,000, but the cost of the house should be calculated on how much it costs a young couple to purchase a house and how much it costs them per month to remain in that house. In our constantly changing social status-and that situation applies to almost every individual in the country-very few families stay on the same social level for long; that is to say, it is only a matter of two or three years until they wish to sell their house and get a larger one or it is only a matter of time until they are obliged to take a job in another town and are therefore faced with the necessity of selling their house. Hence, to all intents and purposes, that house should cost what it cost to move in and what it cost per month to stay there, and getting the equity invested when it is sold.
That is the basic philosophy upon which the United States predicated their housing


program which permits a veteran to purchase a new house without paying anything at all, not even legal costs, to pay nothing for the first two months, and to start monthly payments two months after he moves in. That is the philosophy that permits a young couple in the United States to be able to move into a house that is furnished with about $2,000 worth of built-in furniture, kitchen equipment and so on with $400 down and they start their payments about three months later. Our problem of high down payments is unique to Canada. The same United States housing philosophy applies in England and in most countries whose housing programs I have studied.
The philosophy is based on how much il costs to get into a house and how much it costs to stay there. It is also predicated on the proposition that a citizen is a much better citizen when he owns his own house, when he has title to his own house, regardless ol the amount of the mortgage that is on it, because he owns the house and when he does something to the house he is doing something to enhance the value of the property which he is acquiring month by month. It also gives him a greater interest in the community. It makes for the elimination of slums. It permits families with $3,000 to $4,000 income to buy a house. That is the problem I have in my riding and it is the problem I am going to have until this government realizes that something must be done.
I sometimes get very much discouraged when I go down to my riding and I can tell you that it is not easy for a member of parliament to face his constituents and be obliged to tell them that the only reason why they cannot get houses when they have not the exorbitant down payment required is that our government is following along in the footsteps of the old Liberal regime which we promised to eradicate from Canada as far as housing is concerned.
I feel that the whole philosophy of housing should be studied. The proposition should be put forward and the members of the House of Commons should be permitted to discuss it. Housing should be made available regardless of the down payment and should be made available on the assumption that a person should not be denied the privilege to own his own home merely because his income happens to be below $4,000 or $5,000 a year.
Another thing that enters into the matter is this. I just made a little calculation here a few minutes ago. At this rate of 6f per cent the cost of a $16,000 house over a 25-year period comes to $25,000. I maintain that is too much to pay for a $16,000 house.

Do not forget this fact, Mr. Chairman. These houses in Canada are bare. There is nothing in them apart from the heating equipment. As to all the other built-in kitchen equipment and so on that is included in the United States houses and those in other countries, we do not have the benefit of that at all in Canada. Sometimes I think that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation does not have enough faith in the Canadian people. If the United States government can sponsor legislation which provides these benefits to their people, I see no reason why those benefits cannot be provided to the people of Canada. When I say that, Mr. Chairman, I speak very seriously, I can assure you.
The situation must be studied and it must also be regarded from the point of view of the citizen who does not have a steady salary; and that consideration applies to the vast majority of workers in the maritime provinces who follow the woods or the fishing industries and who do not have a regular weekly pay cheque. I feel that this system as it is now may very well serve the people in other parts of Canada, but it does not serve the people of the maritimes. I refer to urban areas where people are working for a fixed high weekly salary and know every week exactly what they are going to make. They can possibly get along under this system. There is no question that houses are being built under this system. As the minister has just said, this government has built under that system more houses than did the old government. However, the problem down home is that our people have not the down payment. That is the first problem. They cannot afford to pay that high rate of interest; and that is the second problem.
There is only one thing to do with these problems and that is to solve them. I can recall the rather animated discussion that took place in the federal-provincial conference between the Prime Minister and the premier of my province, when the premier of New Brunswick went to great pains to explain how-as I just told the committee this afternoon-our people were in the position in which they could not find the high down payment. That consideration applies to the vast majority of our people. I feel that a new philosophy with regard to housing is a requirement. I urgently request that this government give it immediate consideration.

I know that the hon. member has a point, and that an elderly citizen living in one of these projects cannot afford to pay the rent if his sole income is his old age pension. With great respect, this is one of the sad aspects of life. There are certain elderly citizens who have nothing or more to live on than their old age pensions. However, I think the hon. member for Vancouver East would be one of the first to realize that this is more than a housing problem which he is raising with me at the moment. It is a problem which involves welfare, not only federal, but provincial and municipal welfare as well. projects plus assistance from the welfare organizations so as to take care of the senior citizens in whose welfare the hon. member takes such an interest.

speechtext: I hoped I had made myself clear. We appreciate the problem which the hon. member raises. At the moment I am considering the housing bill.
