Nevertheless, I would be very glad to take up with the senior officials of my department the problems which the hon. member has outlined, namely the desirability of establishing an even lower rent than the one considered to be a low one at the present time with regard to senior citizens' houses. But, of course, no rent is low to a person who cannot afford it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before we go further, I think I should tell hon. members that in my view they cannot expect to have the same latitude in the discussion in committee as they have been allowed on second reading. Up to now some of the comments made with reference to the operation of the act as amended by the bill, or as not amended by the committee, appear to the straying a good deal from the subject under discussion, and I would therefore ask the co-operation of all members of the committee to see that we discuss the bill before us and nothing else.

National Housing Act
Would the minister mind telling us how the present interest rate on limited dividend housing compares with that which was in existence at the time his government took office?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We will be glad to look that up. I just want to say, in passing, that when we raised the interest on loans for housing we did not raise the rate on limited dividend projects. The hon. member for Vancouver East will be glad to hear that.
What is the present rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Five and seven-eighths per cent.
When we started, it was 3J per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I think it was even lower than that at the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In January, 1957, just before the deluge, it was 4J per cent. It is 5| per cent now.
Is it still the principle of the department that on the homes of senior citizens no more than 1 per cent above the borrowing rate to the government should be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: On limited dividend projects it is i per cent above our borrowing rate. The rate is fixed every six months. I remember fixing it not long ago.
Could the minister tell us how many homes were built in 1959, 1958 and in the last half of 1957 with the aid of conventional loans in which C.M.H.C. did not participate?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will be happy to have that information looked up.

Mr. Chairman, I have three questions which I should like to put to the minister on this clause. My first question has to do with small homes for fishermen. Last Friday the minister held up in his hand a pamphlet which he said had to do with the minimum home. I am not sure whether or not that home was especially designed to meet the needs of fishermen but I should be grateful if the minister could tell us how many of the homes have been built in Newfoundland during the last year and the year before, that is 1958 and 1959 separately?
My second question has to do with the position of the province with respect to housing agreements. There are rumours circulating in Newfoundland to the effect that the federal government will not sign any further agreements with respect to housing
[The Chairman.]
with the provincial government until certain actions now before the civil courts have been disposed of. I should be grateful if the minister would clarify what the position is in that respect.
My third question is based on an announcement made by the Minister without Portfolio for Newfoundland a few days ago. As a foundation for my question I should like to quote the first two paragraphs of this press release which is dated Ottawa, March 7:
Approval to investigate a proposed land assembly project involving some 500 acres on the eastern outskirts of St. John's, Newfoundland, was announced here today by Hon. W. J. Browne on behalf of the Hon. David J. Walker, minister responsible for the operations of the federal housing agency, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The investigation into the project will include an examination of acquisition costs, planning studies and a schedule of development. If it is decided to proceed, the development will be arranged under section 36 of the National Housing Act and the slum clearance act, 1950, Newfoundland. Cost of the project would be shared 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the city of St. John's, which would act as agent for the province and assume the full provincial share of costs.
It is the last sentence on which I would like clarification.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I indicated a moment ago that I thought these questions were not relevant to the bill. They could be discussed when the estimates of the department come before us. Questions should relate to the bill before the committee and not to the general application of the act.

Mr. Chairman, with the greatest possible respect, all three of my hon. friend's questions have precisely to do with the question of the purposes for which these loans are to be made. Surely, it is extraordinary that we should be asked to approve a bill to increase vastly the amount of money to be loaned and be denied the chance to question the minister under whose department these loans are to be made about the people to whom the loans are to be made.
In all three of my hon. friend's questions these points were involved. In one of the questions the point was raised whether a different policy would be pursued in one province as opposed to the other provinces in respect of these loans.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I cannot accept the comments of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. If the discussion had taken place at the resolution stage or on second reading possibly the question would have been applicable but hon. members at this stage cannot expect to raise questions that concern the entire housing problem in Canada, and have

them considered relevant. It is my definite view that these questions are out of order.

Mr. Chairman, may I speak to the point of order. I feel that this is a serious matter that has been raised. After all, we are now in the committee stage and are discussing whether or not we ought to vote the minister more money on two different counts, one on the operations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation itself and the other a question of whether the government or the corporation should be permitted to add to the number of insured loans.
If we are being asked to vote more money for the home branch of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I see no purpose in having a committee stage unless in that committee stage we are able to inquire of the minister and receive replies as to the expenditures that are taking place in this department to which we are being asked to grant $500 million more money. That is a lot of money even in terms of the budget of the federal government. I feel the whole intent of the committee stage is lost if we are denied the right to question these expenditures.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, you have suggested that this type of thing could be brought up on second reading, but with great respect, if those questions were asked on second reading there would be no possibility of the minister giving an immediate reply to them. In the committee stage the minister has his officials before him and can get the facts from them. This is exactly the time when we should ask questions as to how the money is to be spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, could I beg your indulgence and be permitted to answer the questions in spite of your ruling? I shall be very glad to do so if I may.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo asked about the fisherman's house. After going around the fishing villages of Newfoundland and finding out about this, I must confess that as far as I am aware there have not been in the fishing villages any applications for these homes. The people there feel that if they are going to get a new home they do not want to be confined to one costing $5,000. They want homes with plumbing and other conveniences and one can appreciate that. I must say the minimum house certainly has not sold well in Newfoundland.
I am glad the hon. member asked his second question. I think very highly of Mayor Mews of St. John's. It is true that we have two lawsuits pending with the province of Newfoundland, one of them concerning Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I have arranged with Mayor Mews to have the Royal
National Housing Act
Bank guarantee the payment for which the province is responsible and, as well, the city of St. John's has made itself responsible so we are no longer dependent on a provincial government upon which we have not been able to depend in the past. We are going ahead at a cost of 75 per cent to ourselves to investigate a very important land assembly project in connection with St. John's where there is a great dearth of housing at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, although the minister answered my first question he did not make clear whether the rumours I referred to are with or without foundation. Is it a fact that no agreements are being signed with the provincial government until these actions are disposed of? Is that the position? His answer would seem to indicate that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: As a matter of fact there would be no agreement in any event until this matter is investigated concerning the land assembly project. As to what the future holds, I would not be in a position to say at the moment because it would depend on circumstances at that time.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could direct a supplementary question to the minister on this highly important point. Is the minister telling us he has not made up his mind whether or not he is going to discriminate against one province? Is that what we are to understand by his answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not a question of discrimination. In Newfoundland we have bent over backwards to assist. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is a very important and flourishing development there. It is not a question of discrimination when one realizes that the province of Newfoundland without any colour of right is withholding more than $400,000 owing to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on matters-[DOT]
Mrr. Pickersgill: Mr. Chairman,-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Would the hon. member let me finish the sentence?
Mr. Chairman, I raise a point of order at this time. I raise a point of order and I am sure the Minister of Public Works would quite agree that-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You can when I finish my sentence if you do not mind.
I am raising a point of order about the sentence the minister is in the course of uttering.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
You do not want to hear the truth.

National Housing Act

My point is that if the minister is discussing something that is now before the courts I should like a ruling before he begins that discussion whether it is a subject that we as well as the minister can discuss.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member-[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sure that the minister, being a learned member of the bar, would not undertake to discuss a matter of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that the matter of the $400,000 owing by the province of Newfoundland to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has no relation to the lawsuit.

Will the minister explain what is involved by the city of St. John's acting as agent for the province? Is that agreement signed between the federal government and the municipality? Does the city undertake provincial responsibilities in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Under this particular section of the act the agreement is ordinarily made between the province and the dominion but here the province has appointed the city of St. John's as agent and the signing will be done by the city of St. John's and the federal government. Does that answer the question?

At this stage I should like to ask the minister to clarify something. He gave us some figures for the months of December, January and February in the last two years. In December, 1958, there were 579 loans by loan and trust companies compared with 117 in December, 1959. In January, 1959 there were 516 loans compared with 140 in January, 1960. In February, 1959 there were 1,043 compared with 550 in February, 1960. That is a total of 2,138 last year compared with 807 this year or a decrease of 1,331 or 62 per cent.
With regard to housing loans by banks the picture is even more serious for the same months. There were 900 in December, 1958 compared with 17 in December, 1959; 670 in January, 1959 compared with 11 in January, 1960; and 883 in February, 1959 compared with 6 in February of 1960. That is a total decrease of 2,419 or 99 per cent. Taking these two fields, there is an average decrease of 82 per cent in one year for those three months. Could the minister let us have the complete over-all picture with respect to all approved lenders' loans made in those three months of the two years so that we can see how the figures compare?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, from the first of January to March 11 last year the number of approved loans by life, loan and trust

companies was 1,916; this year the figure is 1,117. During that period last year the banks made 2,419 loans and this year 17. The total for last year up to March 11 was 4,335 and this year it is 1,134.
Can the minister tell the committee what is the exact aggregate amount of all loans up to date in respect of which insurance policies have been issued under the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The last time I saw the figure, which was over the week end, it was, as I recall, $3.4 billion, but we will look it up and see if we have anything more up to date.
A few moments ago the minister made reference to the minimum home. May I ask him how many of these homes have been built in the other three Atlantic provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We will look that up too.
May I ask the minister if my answer is ready now?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: What was the question?
I asked for the number of homes built without C.M.H.C. participation in 1959, 1958 and the last part of 1957. I asked it about five minutes ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In 1957 conventional mortgages totalled 35,898.
Is that the last half?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We do not have figures for the last half. Last night, in order to reply to the hon. member for Nipissing, I looked up the number of C.M.H.C. loans for the first six months but I have not looked up conventional loans. Do you want that as well?
If you will.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In 1957 conventional loans totalled 35,898. Those who started their homes with mortgages supplied by their friends and not through any approved lender numbered 35,768. They are usually grouped together. In 1958 the number of conventional loans was 44,744 and starts beyond conventional loans totalled 34,838. In 1959 there were 45,000 conventional loans and 34,900 starts without conventional loans. These figures do not include any N.H.A. figures for approved lenders or for C.M.H.C. loans.
At the same time will the minister be good enough to give us a breakdown by provinces of the aggregate amount mentioned a moment ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will have that for you some time tomorrow.

I should like to thank the minister for the figures he gave a moment ago and at the same time to pursue the matter further. Based on the figures the minister gave, there is still a decrease of about 75 per cent. In addition, we have the announced intention of the minister to cut back by 50 per cent the building program of last year. Could the minister tell us on what evidence the government made this decision and if the government feels that the situation is being met? On the one hand, we have a 75 per cent decrease in loans in the first three months of this year compared with last year and on the other hand we have the announced intention of the government to cut back their contribution to the building program by 50 per cent. I have in mind particularly the relationship of the building program to the employment situation and the need of making loans available immediately.
I noticed that the minister said that no builders' loans would be made available until next fall and at that time they would consider whether there was any need to do this. I should also like to know if the minister can inform us whether it is a decision of the Minister of Finance that is preventing proper action. I am sure the minister would like to carry on the very vigorous job done by the previous minister and it certainly does not seem that he is in a position to do so. Could the minister explain the reason for this action? It does not seem that the government is taking a realistic look at the situation at all.

I wonder if the minister would tell us where he obtained the figure he used in his forecast of last night of 80,000 to 85,000 homes built under conventional loans in 1960? I think he explained this was the best advice he could get from a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation survey, but when one looks at Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation housing statistics he finds that the most loans ever made under the conventional plan up to 1958 was 44,744. Would the minister explain this jump from 44,744 in 1958 to 80,000 or 85,000 in 1960?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member for Trinity, may I say that if he will add the figures up, that is the 45,000 plus 34,900, he will find it comes to around the figure of
80,000.
What is this figure of 34,900?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
If the 80,000 are included in the conventional loans, conventional loans through trust companies, mortgage companies and so on at the conventional rates. They represent also the 34,900 starts that
National Housing Act
have been made with loans obtained from other sources, or without loans at all. In any event, it is all included in the all-inclusive term "conventional loans". If my friend would like to call them anything else, he is welcome to do so. I did say last year we had around 80,000, 79,900. This year, with the banks refraining from lending, except to satisfy a few customers, and doing so at the rate of 6 per cent, there will be a greater demand for conventional loans than there has been in the past.

I thank the minister for that. What he is saying now is that what he told us last night was not correct. There is a figure of some 30,000 to 40,000 houses started without assistance from lending institutions, mortgage companies and the trust companies, which he did not tell us about.
Last night the minister also forecast that there would be 35,000 N.H.A. starts in 1960. He made this figure up from two components, the first being his guess that the approved lending institutions would make 20,000 N.H.A. loans and his own Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would make 15,000. I have two questions based on this. First of all, what assurance has the minister the approved lending institutions will make
20,000	loans in 1960? Does he have any survey or any report from them which would indicate this? Second, how does the minister explain the fact that even if that total of 35,000 N.H.A. loans is reached in 1960 this will be the lowest figure in eight years? This is far below anything that has been done by either his government, which boasts so much about so little, or the former government, for years. In fact, one has to turn the clock back to 1951 to equal that number.
What he has just told us, in fact, is that he is driving the Canadian people into a position where they will have to go and get conventional loans, at a high cost, in order to build their houses. How does the minister relate this to his supposed interest in the little man who wants to get a home but who cannot afford the high interest rates? How can he justify the fact he is only planning for 35,000 National Housing Act loans in 1960, which is far below anything that has been done for eight years? Why is he going to force these little Canadian home purchasers, the people who need houses, to go and get their money from the lending institutions, through conventional mortgages, at rates which the minister knows are much higher than N.H.A. rates? He said so proudly earlier that he would not like to see N.H.A. rates fluctuate, but at the same time he is going to force tens of thousands of Canadians

National Housing Act to get smaller loans at higher interest rates and then, because they cannot afford to finish their houses on that basis, they will have to get second and third mortgages and pay 20 per cent or 25 per cent per annum on this money. Is this the present government's policy?

I wonder if I might ask the minister a few questions along the same lines as those asked by the hon. member for Trinity. I noticed that on page 1995 of Hansard for March 11, 1960, the minister had this to say:
We have confidence that this rate-
He had reference to the new interest rate of 6|- per cent.
-will attract the approved lenders back into the field.
I should like to ask the minister where he obtained the assurance that these lenders are going to re-enter the field as a result of the rise in interest rates. I believe the minister is aware that his colleague, the Minister of Finance, only yesterday floated a bond issue which would yield to the purchaser 5.99 per cent plus a few added extras that were in there for the benefit of the buyer of the bonds. Is the minister telling us that an investment house is going to show any interest in making an insured loan under this act and be satisfied with 6.75 per cent if it can obtain a bond on the open market and realize 5.99 per cent plus extras? Is he telling us that any company is going to be interested in a difference of .76 of 1 per cent, and is going to be willing to have its money out on loan for as long as 25 years and have operating expenses, collections and everything else that is involved, for this small difference? I think the minister ought now to give us additional assurance, rather than the blanket statement that he has confidence this rate will bring lenders into the field.
All the indications are, as the minister has revealed them, that there has been a reduction in loans of 70 per cent to 85 per cent. We are getting a little confused by the various statistics the minister is giving us, but the indication is fairly clear that there has been a reduction of approximately 75 per cent. Yet the minister says he is expecting about the same level of housing in this year as last year. I should like to ask the minister also how he can account for the mortgage companies or investment houses being willing to make these loans at a rate of 6J per cent, when they could lend out all the money they want to lend out for housing in first class mortgages on their own terms and receive the going rate of 8 per cent. The


minister reads the newspapers, and I know he has read all the reliable accounts in the Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver newspapers indicating that the going rate is 8 per cent. Does he mean to say that these companies are going to show any interest whatever in these long term mortgages at lower interest rates?
I think the minister, if he will take us into his confidence, will have to make the admission that housing and the other social needs of the Canadian people simply cannot compete on the open money market with industrial enterprises for the available investment capital of the nation. We are only deluding ourselves if we imagine that by raising the interest rate a little bit, which makes it far too high for the low income people to pay and yet not nearly high enough to produce the money, we are going to make this field attractive to the private companies. We will find that the Canadian people who need housing the most have had to sacrifice their housing needs, not in order to help the Minister of Finance balance his budget but to help him out in his predicament in regard to his cash position.
I realize the minister is right when he says this has nothing to do with the budget. We realize it may have very little to do with balancing the budget but it certainly has a great deal to do with the cash position of the government of Canada at the present time. I should like the minister at this time to present us with some evidence or some indication of why he says he is confident that this rate will attract the lenders back to this field. I am sure the minister must have some reason for making such a claim and that it is not merely based on political optimism.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not know how many times we have to explain these things to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I am glad to see that he is another example of conflict in that party. He would like to see a higher rate than 6| per cent.
I said no such thing. It is the minister who is making that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission

speechtext: That is a lie.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You have not indicated which rate you would prefer. Tell us what rate you prefer.
Three per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Three per cent for the leader and more than 6J per cent for all the rest of the party.
That is another lie.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Assini-boia should stick to wheat. He becomes more ridiculous as the hours pass.
This is the most discourteous member of the cabinet.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May the hon. member not lose his temper.
Who is losing his temper?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: He also suggested that I was good-natured as well and very genial. I hope he does not change that opinion in this committee.
Just stick to the truth for a change.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member must be a good farmer. I am sure he has a model farm. Some time I am going out to look at it, because he must be specializing in something but certainly it has not been housing.
May I now answer the hon. member for Trinity? It is a wonderful thing to hear him, an aristocratic builder in Toronto who appeals to the people in the big money brackets, talking for the first time today about the poor unfortunate people. He is the one who has suggested to the House of Commons that we should not have a fixed rate of 6} per cent but that we should have a floating rate of 7J per cent or 7J per cent, the same as on the conventional loans. The interjections of
National Housing Act
the hon. member for Trinity remind me of the time when he was in the house making somewhat the same plea on behalf of Avro. I do not know whom he is representing now but certainly he himself is a builder and represents the big interests in building.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not think the suggestion he makes here requires an answer except by the poor unfortunate people in whom he is for the first time showing an interest.
Yesterday when I spoke in this committee I did so in a completely constructive vein and I am disappointed-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You changed today.

Yes; I have changed today. I am disappointed that the minister, instead of paying some attention to the constructive suggestions I put forward, embarked on a course of recrimination and political haymaking.
Personalities.

His wind-up speech last night was political and not factual. In it there were figures which had distortions, as he told us today, of 100 per cent. He said the same type of thing on television last night. How he managed to get on television and to make that bland, fatuous assurance to the Canadian people, I have no knowledge whatsoever. But I admit that I am disappointed. We were trying to help him to resolve a situation or mess which his government got him into. Instead of being grateful for the assistance he has turned on us and has tried to make us look as though we were not interested in the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Are you?

We certainly are. Let me just indicate one or two of the things the minister has commented on. He chided me for suggesting that the banks should be allowed to make National Housing Act loans. I make no apology for this suggestion. As a matter of fact, I think the minister is protecting the banks. I think he is back to the old Conservative policy of protecting the vested interests.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: You are a childish little boy.

The truth of the matter is that the banks do not want to make N.H.A. loans at the present time and they are using this government as a shield. What is actually happening, as I understand it, is the following. A little buyer in one of these small towns all across the country goes in to the bank manager and says, "I should like to get a loan; I want a loan under the N.H.A." The

National Housing Act
bank manager says to him, "Mr. Smith, I should like to make you an N.H.A. loan; nothing would give me greater pleasure; but unfortunately I cannot do it because it is government policy that the banks are not permitted to make N.H.A. loans at the current interest rate. Of course, if the government changes its policy and amends the act, I shall be pleased to send in an application for a loan for you right away but at the present time I am not able to do so and no one is sorrier than I am."
Mr. Chairman, you will recall that last summer, the Prime Minister made a statement about the banks which did not please them at all. There are some bankers who would like to make N.H.A. loans but there are some-a small minority-who never have enjoyed being in the business and who do not want to get back into it again. These are the most conservative bankers, and they are now asking for protection from my hon. friend and his colleagues.
The real point of this whole matter, however, is that the loans which the banks do not make to their small customers in the little towns all across the country will have to be made by someone else, and the someone else will make them at a higher rate than 6| per cent or 6f per cent, let there be no mistake about that. The loans will be from the insurance companies at 7J per cent or 8 per cent and they will be from other lending sources in the small towns at 9 per cent or 10 per cent and on second and third mortgages once again at this exorbitant interest-shark rate of 15 per cent, 20 per cent or 25 per cent per annum. Is this what the government is trying to accomplish?
Surely suggesting means whereby individual borrowers from coast to coast may have additional offices in which they can apply for and obtain N.H.A. loans is in the interests of the Canadian people. I am surprised and disappointed that my hon. friend would impute any motives because it is beneath him to do so. It is beneath him to suggest that I ever had anything but the best interests of the Canadian people and the workers at Avro at heart when I spoke on their behalf. I have never been on the payroll of any company other than the one for which I was working in my whole life. I resent the minister or anyone else making false accusations against me.
The minister has not answered my question [DOT]-and I wish he would do so-as to what makes him think the approved lenders this year will make 20,000 loans. After he has given us some assurance on that score, he has still to tell us why, when there were 85,000 N.H.A. loans in 1958, it is going to be sufficient to have 35,000 N.H.A. loans in 1960.

Why the decrease of 50,000 N.H.A. loans? Is this what the Canadian people want? Are there 50,000 less Canadians who are going to need N.H.A. assistance in 1960 than there were in 1958, or is it the policy of the government to make the 50,000 Canadains go out into the market and borrow their money at higher interest rates?

Mr. Chairman, I cannot allow the minister's statement in regard to my attendance to remain unanswered. I would like to place the minister in the position of one of us in our group where, instead of having to handle only one third of the opposition, he would have three cabinet ministers plus hundreds of senior advisers to handle. I can assure the minister that I have spent more hours on the subject of housing since the house opened than the minister has, and even though I may not have been in the house during every moment of the last few days, I have been organizing the housing debate on behalf of our group and I know every word that the minister has uttered in this house on the question of housing. I have before me notes of what the minister has had to say and they are covered with ink. I could speak for hours and hours on some of the faulty impressions which the minister created on this subject of housing, but I will not.
I do want to clear up very definitely what our policy is with regard to interest rates for housing. The minister has on a number of occasions said that members of this group advocate a higher interest rate for housing, but the minister has no evidence of that fact. As a matter of fact, last night he said that my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena, had advocated an even higher interest rate, but let me inform the minister that that hon. member has not yet said one word in this debate. So the minister was completely off the beam there.
However, I do contend that it is the actions of the government which are forcing people to pay 8 per cent, and on second mortgages as high as a yield of 30 per cent, in order to obtain the capital required for their housing needs. The minister has explained to the house exactly what will happen to an applicant for an N.H.A. loan. In the first instance the minister seemed worried about the 82,000 homes which obviously have not found a buyer yet, and first of all the applicant is going to be sent to look over these 82,000 homes. That is an odd attitude for a government to take. Why should the government in the face of continuously rising costs of housing and rentals attempt to come to the aid of those who have, unfortunately, built homes for which there may not be a ready market? The government is now going to bail out these

builders and force all the would-be home owners to go and look over 82,000 homes now on the market. This is-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want my hon. friend to be under any misconception. There is no fault in the 82,000 homes. They are not completed and therefore could not be sold. They are coming on to the market.

Even if they are uncompleted, it is a new attitude for the government to take to advise a Canadian citizen that the blessings of the act shall not extend to him or be extended to him until he has seen whether or not he can accommodate himself in one of these houses now being built. If the proposed 82,000 homes are unacceptable to the would-be buyer, the minister told us that the applicant will then have to go to an approved lender, and after having been turned down by this lender, if the man's income is low enough and he satisfies several other qualifications, I might say not inconsiderable qualifications, then and only then will the government give serious consideration, not to allowing him to buy an N.H.A. mortgage- oh no-but to allowing him the privilege of applying for one of these direct loans.
The minister can see for himself the stumbling blocks the government is setting up for the would-be home owner in Canada which are going to force most of the people in Canada to go to the regular lending institutions to get help for their housing needs. There they will have to pay these excessively high interest rates which, in view of the high capital cost of housing today, the average working man and woman of Canada is completely unable to afford. It is another beautiful handout by this government to the moneylenders of Canada, and the people of Canada who need housing loans at a modest rate of interest are in fact being asked to help the Minister of Finance balance his cash position by the time the budget is presented to this house.
I should also like to refer the minister to resolution No. 30 on the order paper in my name on behalf of this group. After calling for a national investment board, we ask that the board shall, among other things-
Make capital available at an interest rate of not more than 3 per cent for socially necessary projects such as housing and development requirements of municipalities.
That has always been our position, that capital should be made available at or near cost, and if necessary at a subsidized interest rate to meet the housing needs of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, just a few brief comments. I got the impression from the hon. member for Trinity that there must be as
National Housing Act
many views of bank managers as there are of hon. members in this house. After listening to the hon. member I can tell him that, although I may be a proletariat member of this house, I also do a lot of checking, investigating and talking, and in Vancouver the bank managers told me that there was one reason only that they were not lending money, and that was because they did not have the money to lend.

If the hon. member reads my speech of last night he will read the qualification I put in. I had said that there were individual exceptions where loans would be made, and they could at least make them or not make them at their own discretion, which is what they cannot do now.

I am talking of what the hon. member said ten minutes ago. Believe it or not, I am on pretty darned good terms with bank managers because I do not borrow from them.
I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works a couple of questions under clause 1 which are of importance, I think, and I hope the minister can give the answers. In view of the bill before us and the amount of money which is being asked for, has the minister or his staff in front of him any information as to what are now the construction costs of homes as compared with about a year or two years ago, and also the cost of rents in the last year or two? The reason I ask is that if there has been an increase in the cost of construction of homes in the last 12 or 24 months and also an increase in rents over that same period, would it have any bearing in the minister's mind on the need for a greater expansion in home and apartment construction? If so, how does he relate that to a reduction in the amount of money which is being made available under this bill? Would the minister mind answering those questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend for Vancouver East, there was some increase in 1959 in the cost of dwellings financed under the act. Land costs were up about 3 per cent, bringing the cost of the average lot to $2,533. That is, N.H.A. loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Construction costs per square foot increased by 2.6 per cent with little change in area. These increases brought the average cost of houses built by builders or owners in 1959 to $13,181 under the small home loans arrangements, and $15,896 for dwellings financed by approved lenders.

I recognize the minister's sincerity. In view of that, is the hon. gentleman, or his department, or any phase of

National Housing Act
government, to his knowledge giving any thought to taking action to stop speculation on subdivisions, and buying and selling lots acquired under the terms of the National Housing Act? I know for a fact that the price of lots has gone up from $250 to $3,000. Is there no control over the money which is advanced under N.H.A. especially if it is being used to pay for land acquired under a speculative building program? I read day after day about what is happening outside Toronto, for instance, where farms are being sold for $500,000, a million dollars and so on. Has the minister or his department any control over that at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Unfortunately that is a matter of property and civil rights over which the dominion government has no control. The costs do constitute a problem for Central Mortgage and Housing. As the hon. member says, many people have made fortunes by buying farms and dividing them. It makes our problem difficult, because a much higher percentage of the ordinary man's capital has to go toward paying for a lot.
Is there any public control over this, or does the matter fall completely under provincial jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I fear it does.
Did the minister just say he wished they had control over property and civil rights?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Central Mortgage and Housing would sometimes like to have that so that we could hold down the price of lots and put the money into the actual construction of homes. It is just a whim. I am not suggesting we should change the British North America Act.

I am exceedingly disappointed that the minister seems to be taking so casual a view about the importance in the past of the commercial banks in the housing lending field. While he is sneering not only at the hon. member for Trinity, and others who made constructive suggestions to him and is sneering at the previous administration, I suggest he should do some homework and take a look at some of the activities in connection with N.H.A. loans before he assumed responsibility. The hon. gentleman does not need to take my word as to what went on in 1957. I suggest, in relation to lending by the banks that he would find a good tip by reading what was reported by the governor of the Bank of Canada who reported to the new Minister of Finance in 1958 with respect to the activities of the bank before the election in 1957.

If the minister will read what appears on page 28 of the Bank of Canada report for 1957 he will find that it seems the commercial banks were reluctant to take proper responsibility with respect to lending for house construction in this country then despite the change in the Bank Act which was made in 1954 to enable them to do so. This is what the governor of the Bank of Canada had to say about what was done at that time, and I suggest that the minister might study this report carefully, because some action of the same kind might be taken at the present time. I am reading from page 28 of the governor's report for 1957:
In discussing this situation with the chartered banks I expressed the view that they should maintain continuity in mortgage lending as an important field of investment for savings entrusted to them. At a meeting in March the banks agreed to resume operations m this field on much the same scale as in 1956, the objective being new housing loans in 1957 in a total amount of not less than $150 million, involving approximately 15,000 units; the Bank of Canada indicated that the total resources of the banks as a group could be expected to increase during 1957 by an amount at least great enough to take care of their disbursements on mortgage loans in that year, so that it would not be necessary for the banks to dispose of other assets in order to maintain a flow of funds for insured housing loans. In the event, the banks approved 15,700 mortgage loans during 1957 valued at $173 million-
I suggest, as the hon. member for Trinity has suggested, that the chartered banks of this country are the lenders who can be reached by the residents in the countless small towns of Canada. There are hundreds and hundreds of branch banks across this country in places in which other approved housing lenders like the mortgage companies and the insurance companies have no interest whatever. But the banks now are not making a contribution to the construction of houses. In addition-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? The hon. member for Trinity complained that I was a friend of the banks. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River says I am sneering at the banks. I appreciate the role of the banks, and I regret very much that at the present time-
I did not say you were sneering at the banks but rather at their importance as lenders in this field.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Is the hon. member in favour of raising the interest rates of the banks to 6J per cent?

What I am suggesting is that the minister and Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada have a meeting with the banks and do what was done early in 1957, when the banks had departed from the house lending market,

with the result that 15,700 houses were constructed. Alter the meeting, I think, the minister should come back to this chamber and indicate what might be necessary in order that housing loans may be made through the agencies of these banks in small communities all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: At 6J per cent?

I did not say what the interest rate would be. On the earlier point, I did not say the minister was sneering at the banks. What I did say was that the hon. gentleman gave the impression of sneering at the importance of bank lending in the housing field and sneered at the absence of the banks from this field at the present time.
What has also alarmed me is that the minister says he is not proposing to make direct loans to individual home owners unless they can establish that they are not able to get loans from other approved lenders. This is going to mean a tremendous run-around as far as the communities I represent are concerned. We know they are not going to be able to get any loans in the present climate from commercial banks in any of these communities.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member must be out of touch. For the last two years we have been doing that; we have been asking applicants for loans to go first to the approved lenders. If the hon. member did not know this, I can only tell him it is a fact.
I have been well aware of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Are you objecting to it?

No. The point I am making is that the nearest approved lender has been, in fact, in small communities a branch of the chartered banks. People in Kenora-Rainy River have known for some years that it is useless to go, for example, to the city of Winnipeg, which is anywhere between 150 to 300 miles away, to apply to any of the insurance companies expecting them to take an interest in housing loans in a small town. The insurance companies are completely occupied by their lending policies in the large centres where loans can be administered in wholesale quantities much more cheaply than in small towns hundreds of miles distant from head office in major cities.
My point is that the minister has intimated that the banks are out of this field. He gave figures to me on Friday last showing that in February of last year the banks had made 883 loans whereas in February of this year they made only 6 loans.
National Housing Act
In other words, the bank type of approved lender who has proved useful to the dwellers in these small communities is out of business now. My point is that if these people then have to go to another approved lender, presumably an insurance company several hundred miles away from where they live they know they are going to be turned down. But I say the minister is asking them to go through a useless run-around motion before they can go to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and ask for a direct loan.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to take exception to the remarks made by the minister both in this chamber and outside of it. He has indulged in a complete distortion of facts and has attempted to treat in a political way a very important situation. I am not going to refer to his television performance last evening which I must confess I did not see but I am told that he made a strong political presentation.
Last evening the minister attempted to leave the impression that since this government had taken office and because of the actions of the government 400,000 homes had been built. We have the figures today showing that all the housing, outside of N.H.A. housing, amounted to more than one half of that figure he used last evening. There has been a complete distortion of the facts. The minister last evening also went on to say that due to the winter works program of the Prime Minister 82,000 homes were being built. There is a confusing statement and the minister should not have attempted to drag in the winter works program which has absolutely nothing to do with this subject.
I rose to speak briefly at this time simply because I did not want to let this occasion pass without pointing out these very misleading statements made by the minister who ran out of the chamber in the middle of the debate on second reading to get on a national television network and give a onesided distorted view of the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, obviously the hon. member for Nipissing did not hear my broadcast. There were no misstatements. It was very accurate.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group are most interested in this bill and will support right down the line any expenditure that will aid in the construction of homes in Canada. We are, of course, disappointed in the amount in clause 1 and in what we say we are trying to get explanations of policy from the minister.
I speak from memory, but I believe with respect to insurance that it amounts to 2 per cent of N.H.A. loans. There is something

National Housing Act
in the neighbourhood of $60 million. I believe that is the figure. I understand that the interest return on the operations of the act since its inauguration is considerable. Are the interest payments under the N.H.A. to Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation held in trust and invested in government bonds? Is the insurance which I am told amounts to $60 million held in trust? Could the interest paid on money advanced by N.H.A. up to now which is well over $1 billion and the money from insurance now be applied, not on the investment of government bonds but as a revolving fund for investment in new housing in addition to what the minister is now asking for authority to spend?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member, the interest and principal goes back each year to the consolidated revenue fund. It is paid by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation back to the Receiver General of Canada. In 1958 the return on principal and interest amounted to $71.4 million; in 1958 it amounted to $85.5 million; and in 1959 it amounted to $110 million. There is not a revolving fund. As the money is received it goes back to the consolidated revenue fund.
In connection with the insurance, there is also a trust fund of an additional $63 million,
not $60 million as the hon. member mentioned. It has now reached that figure. That is a very small amount to insure over $3.4 billion worth of loans. After all, this has not been in operation very long.
The whole problem of returning the principal and interest to the consolidated revenue fund was part of the National Housing Act of 1954 and part of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act as well. It was a creation of the former government which seems to be working in the way I described.

That raises the point I was about to deal with. May I call it six o'clock?
Progress reported.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the house leader would be good enough to indicate whether the order of business announced last night will be the same for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, we will continue with this bill and then take the items which I outlined last night. The business for Friday will depend on the progress we make tomorrow.
